title: DevPath
subtitle: First line of code to hireable mid-level CRUD web developer
targetRole: Mid-level full-stack developer building CRUD web applications on JavaScript/TypeScript + React + Node, and C# + ASP.NET Core.
notOnThisPath: Algorithm puzzles and LeetCode grinding. Nothing here asks you to invert a binary tree. The drills are the things teams actually ask about: how HTTP works, why your effect runs twice, what a scoped DI lifetime is, why the API is doing 400 queries per page load.

stages.title: Programming, actually
stages.goal: Write, run and debug a small JavaScript program without copying it from anywhere.
stages.outcome: You can read a short program and predict what it prints.

modules.title: Values, variables, and branching
modules.why: Every bug you will ever write starts with a value not being the type or shape you assumed. JavaScript is unusually willing to convert things behind your back, so this is where you build the instinct.
interviewFocus: == vs === and when coercion bites
let vs const vs var and block scope
Falsy values, and why || 50 is not the same as ?? 50

modules.title: Strings, loops, and counting things
modules.why: Most CRUD work is reshaping one collection of data into another. Loops and string handling are the raw motion you will repeat for the rest of your career.
interviewFocus: Why string indexes and Unicode disagree
for..of vs for..in vs forEach
Building a frequency map with an object vs a Map

steps.title: Count characters — Map vs object, and the __proto__ trap
Text to hex — input validation at the edge

modules.title: Functions, scope, and closures
modules.why: Closures are the single most-asked JavaScript interview topic, and they are also the thing that makes React hooks make sense later. Learn them here and Stage 5 gets much easier.
interviewFocus: What a closure is, in one sentence, with an example
Hoisting: function declarations vs let/const in the temporal dead zone
What `this` refers to, and how arrow functions change it

steps.title: Rock paper scissors — rules as data, separate from I/O
Best stock trade — naming intermediate values

modules.title: Arrays, objects, and copying
modules.why: Accidental shared references cause a whole genre of bug that looks like magic — you change one thing and something unrelated changes too. React state bugs are usually this bug wearing a hat.
interviewFocus: Shallow vs deep copy, and what the spread operator actually does
map / filter / reduce, and which ones mutate

steps.title: Handbook §4–5 — arrays, objects, Map and Set
Array utils — the sort traps and friends
Deep equal — how equality really works

stages.title: Code that survives contact with a team
stages.tagline: The habits that separate a beginner from a junior
stages.goal: Write code someone else can change next month without breaking it, and prove it with tests.
stages.outcome: You instinctively split pure logic from side effects, and you write a test before you write the fix.

modules.title: Separate deciding from doing
modules.why: This is the whole repo in one idea. Pure functions are testable; functions that print, fetch, or touch the DOM are not. Every architecture pattern you will be asked about is a longer way of saying this.
interviewFocus: What makes a function pure, and why you would want that
Side effects: name three, and where they belong in an app
How you would make untestable code testable without rewriting it

modules.title: Data-driven code and plug-in shapes
modules.why: When adding a feature means adding a row to a table instead of an `else if` to a growing chain, you have designed well. Interviewers probe this with 'how would you add a new payment provider'.
interviewFocus: Replacing a switch with a lookup table, and when not to
Programming to an interface in a language without interfaces
The rule of three: when to generalise

steps.title: Cipher suite — every plug-in has the same shape
State machine — states as data, not booleans
Event emitter — decoupling with a pub/sub seam

modules.title: Designing a function's API
modules.why: Boolean-flag soup (`send(true, false, true)`) is a real thing real codebases have, and cleaning it up is a very common first ticket for a new hire.
interviewFocus: Options object vs positional parameters
Sensible defaults and how to express 'not provided'
Why a function that returns data beats one that prints it

steps.title: Password generator — options objects vs flag soup
Date utils — the worst API in the standard library
Money and carts — never store money in a float

modules.title: Errors, validation, and invariants
modules.why: Junior code throws strings and swallows exceptions. Mid-level code has an error strategy: what fails loudly, what is recoverable, and what the user sees. This comes up in almost every backend interview.
interviewFocus: Custom Error subclasses and why `instanceof` beats string matching
Where validation belongs — edge of the system, not sprinkled through it
Fail fast vs return a Result: the trade-off

steps.title: Custom errors — an error type per failure mode
Validator — collect every problem, not just the first
Bank account — encapsulation protects an invariant

modules.title: Testing, for real
modules.why: Writing a tiny test framework is the fastest way to stop finding tests mysterious. After this you will never again be unsure what a mock is.
interviewFocus: Unit vs integration vs end-to-end, and the rough ratio you'd aim for
What a test double is: stub, mock, fake, spy
What makes a test brittle, and how to fix it

steps.title: Guide — a testing strategy you can defend in an interview
Build a test framework in 100 lines
Test runner v2 — async tests, hooks, reporters

stages.title: The browser, without a framework
stages.tagline: Learn what React is doing for you before you let it
stages.goal: Build an interactive page with plain JavaScript, holding state in data rather than in the DOM.
stages.outcome: You can explain what React actually buys you, because you have done it by hand.

modules.title: State lives in data, not in the DOM
modules.why: The single most important lesson before React. If you learn React first you will cargo-cult it; if you learn this first, hooks are obvious.
interviewFocus: Why reading state back out of the DOM is a bug factory
render(state) as a function — what that means
Event delegation and why you would use it

steps.title: Handbook §10 — the DOM in two pages
To-do app — render as a function of state
Undo/redo — state history as a data structure

modules.title: Events, timing, and responsive interfaces
modules.why: Debounce and throttle are asked about constantly, usually via 'the search box fires a request on every keystroke — fix it'.
interviewFocus: Debounce vs throttle: the difference, in one sentence each
Why you cancel a timer in a cleanup, and what leaks if you don't
Bubbling, capturing, and stopPropagation

steps.title: Debounce and throttle — write both from scratch
Search as you type — debounce plus request cancellation

modules.title: Modules, bundlers, and how code gets to the browser
modules.why: Every frontend job assumes you know why there is a build step. 'What does a bundler do' is a standard warm-up question and a surprising number of candidates cannot answer it.
interviewFocus: ESM vs CommonJS, and why the difference still hurts in Node
What a bundler, a transpiler and a minifier each do
Tree shaking, code splitting, source maps

steps.title: Guide — npm, lockfiles, bundlers and the build step
Markdown previewer — a real multi-module app

stages.title: Async and the network
stages.goal: Fetch data correctly: sequenced, cancelled, retried, rate-limited, and with errors handled.
stages.outcome: You can explain the event loop and debug a race condition on purpose rather than by shuffling awaits.

modules.title: The event loop and promises
modules.why: 'Explain the event loop' and 'what does this print' with a setTimeout/Promise mix are near-universal JS interview questions. Building a promise from scratch makes them trivial.
interviewFocus: Call stack, task queue, microtask queue — and which wins
Why an await inside a loop is often a performance bug
Promise.all vs allSettled vs race vs any

steps.title: Handbook §8 — asynchrony and the five async traps

modules.title: How HTTP actually works
modules.why: This is the highest-value non-code topic on the whole path. Status codes, headers, caching and CORS come up in frontend, backend and fullstack interviews alike.
interviewFocus: GET vs POST vs PUT vs PATCH, idempotency and safety
What each status code family means, and 401 vs 403
What a CORS preflight is and what actually fixes it

steps.title: Guide — HTTP from the wire up
Guide — what the browser does with a URL

modules.title: Consuming an API without lying to your users
modules.why: Loading states, error states, retries, cancellation, pagination. Getting all five right is exactly the gap between a bootcamp portfolio app and production code.
interviewFocus: Retry with exponential backoff — and which errors you must not retry
How you cancel an in-flight request, and why it matters
Cursor vs offset pagination, and when offset breaks

steps.title: Retry and timeout — backoff done properly
Paginated API — async iterators over pages
Weather CLI — a real network client end to end
Rate limiter — token bucket, from scratch

stages.title: TypeScript
stages.tagline: Make wrong programs fail to compile
stages.goal: Model your domain in types well enough that whole categories of bug become impossible.
stages.outcome: You can type an API boundary, narrow a union exhaustively, and write a generic that isn't `any` in disguise.

modules.title: Why types, and how inference works
modules.why: Almost every JS job posting now says TypeScript. The first thing an interviewer checks is whether you use it or just sprinkle `: any` until the red squiggles stop.
interviewFocus: Structural vs nominal typing — TypeScript is structural, and what that implies
`any` vs `unknown` vs `never`
What TypeScript does NOT do at runtime

steps.title: Strictness flags — what each one buys you

modules.title: Modelling data and absence
modules.why: Null handling is where most runtime crashes live. TypeScript can eliminate them, but only if you model optional fields honestly instead of asserting them away.
interviewFocus: Optional property vs `| undefined` — they are not the same
Why `as` is a promise you make to the compiler, and `satisfies` isn't
Interfaces vs type aliases: the real differences

steps.title: Shared interfaces — one source of truth

modules.title: Unions, narrowing, and exhaustiveness
modules.why: Discriminated unions are the single most useful TypeScript pattern for CRUD apps — they model 'loading | error | loaded' and Redux-style actions, and they make the compiler catch the case you forgot.
interviewFocus: Discriminated union — what it is and why the tag matters
How you make a switch exhaustive with `never`
Type guards and `is` predicates

modules.title: Generics you would actually write
modules.why: Interviewers ask for a typed `pick`, a typed cache, or a typed fetch wrapper. Not conditional-type wizardry — just generics that carry a type through a function honestly.
interviewFocus: When a generic is genuinely needed vs when it's noise
Constraints with `extends`, and `keyof`
Why `Array<T>` methods lose type information if you're careless

steps.title: Utility types — Pick, Omit, Partial, Record

modules.title: Typing the boundary: data you did not create
modules.why: The compiler cannot check JSON that arrives over the network. Knowing where types stop being guarantees — and validating there — is a genuinely mid-level skill.
interviewFocus: Why the response of `fetch().json()` is a lie if you type it directly
Runtime validation vs compile-time types — you need both
The Result type vs throwing

stages.title: React
stages.tagline: The frontend half of a CRUD app
stages.goal: Build the screens a CRUD product needs: lists, forms, detail views, optimistic updates, routing.
stages.outcome: You can defend every render your component does, and your effects have no races and no leaks.

modules.title: Components, props, and lists
modules.why: Keys and list rendering produce the most common React bug on earth: state attaching to the wrong row after a delete.
interviewFocus: What the `key` prop is for — and why index-as-key breaks
Props vs state: how you decide
Why `{items.length && <List/>}` renders a stray 0

modules.title: State, and where it belongs
modules.why: Lifting state, colocating state, and never mutating it. Get this wrong and the app becomes unmaintainable at about the fifth screen.
interviewFocus: Why you must not mutate state, in terms of how React decides to re-render
Lifting state up vs colocating it — the trade-off
Derived state: why storing it is usually a bug

modules.title: Effects, fetching, and races
modules.why: The fetch race — type fast in a search box, get results for the wrong query — is asked about constantly and gets fixed wrong just as often.
interviewFocus: What the dependency array really is, and what happens when you lie to it
Effect cleanup: what it's for, when it runs
How you fix a fetch race (two acceptable answers)
When you should NOT use an effect

steps.title: You probably don't need an effect

modules.title: Custom hooks
modules.why: 'Have you written a custom hook?' is a standard mid-level filter question. The good answer describes extracting stateful logic, not just moving code.
interviewFocus: The rules of hooks, and the reason behind them (hook call order)
When to extract a custom hook
useRef for values that shouldn't trigger a render

steps.title: Refs for values, not just DOM

modules.title: Forms, validation, and submission
modules.why: Every CRUD app is mostly forms. Validation timing, submit states, server errors mapped back to fields — this is the daily work of the job you're aiming at.
interviewFocus: Controlled vs uncontrolled inputs, and when uncontrolled is right
Where validation lives when the server validates too
Preventing a double submit

modules.title: The CRUD screens themselves
modules.why: A searchable, sortable, paginated table and a shopping cart are the two most requested take-home exercises in the industry. Build both.
interviewFocus: Sorting and filtering: derive, don't duplicate
Where you put 'selected row' state
URL as state — why filters belong in the query string

modules.title: Composition, context, and component APIs
modules.why: Prop drilling and context misuse are the two ways React apps rot. Interviewers ask 'when would you reach for context' and the wrong answer is 'instead of Redux'.
interviewFocus: Context: what it solves, what it costs (every consumer re-renders)
Compound components and the children pattern
Controlled vs uncontrolled component APIs

modules.title: Performance, honestly
modules.why: Sprinkling `useMemo` everywhere is a junior tell. Knowing when memoisation does nothing — and how to measure — is a mid-level tell.
interviewFocus: What React.memo compares, and why it often doesn't help
useMemo vs useCallback — same idea, different shape
How you would actually find a slow render

modules.title: Accessibility and testable components
modules.why: 'How do you make a modal accessible' separates people who have shipped from people who have not. Focus trapping and keyboard navigation are concrete, learnable, and asked about.
interviewFocus: Focus management in a modal, and what aria-* actually does
Keyboard navigation expectations for a menu
How you test a component without testing React itself

steps.title: Capstone — the whole thing at once

stages.title: The backend, in Node
stages.goal: Build a REST API with authentication, a database, validation, and a sane error contract.
stages.outcome: You can design and defend the API a frontend team would have to consume.

modules.title: Node, npm, and the runtime
modules.why: Frontend devs moving to fullstack routinely get caught by 'what's different about Node vs the browser'. It's an easy question to nail.
interviewFocus: What Node has that the browser doesn't, and vice versa
dependencies vs devDependencies vs peerDependencies
What a lockfile guarantees, and what semver ranges do to you

steps.title: Guide — the Node runtime and the npm ecosystem
Streaming — process a file bigger than RAM

modules.title: Designing and building a REST API
modules.why: This is the centre of gravity of the whole path. Resource naming, status codes, validation, and a consistent error shape.
interviewFocus: How you'd design endpoints for a resource with a sub-resource
Where to return 400 vs 404 vs 409 vs 422
Why PUT should be idempotent and PATCH usually isn't
Versioning an API without breaking clients

steps.title: Guide — REST API design that survives review

modules.title: SQL and relational data
modules.why: The biggest hole in self-taught developers' knowledge, and the one interviewers probe hardest for CRUD roles. You will be asked to write a JOIN.
interviewFocus: INNER vs LEFT JOIN, with a case where the difference matters
What an index does, and why adding one to every column is wrong
Transactions and what ACID means in practice
The N+1 query problem — how you'd spot and fix it
Normalisation, and a defensible reason to denormalise

steps.title: Guide — SQL you will be asked to write
Guide — modelling data, keys and relationships
A tiny database — build the storage layer yourself

modules.title: Authentication and authorization
modules.why: Every CRUD app has a login. Getting it wrong is the most consequential mistake a junior can ship, so interviewers ask carefully.
interviewFocus: Sessions vs JWT — the real trade-off, including logout
Why you hash passwords with bcrypt/argon2 and not SHA-256
Where a token should live in the browser, and the XSS/CSRF trade-off
Authentication vs authorization, with an example of each failing

steps.title: Guide — auth, sessions, tokens and cookies
Guide — the security basics you're expected to know

modules.title: Realtime and the fullstack join
modules.why: WebSockets show up in enough job specs to be worth a day, and building a collaborative feature forces you to think about state on two machines at once.
interviewFocus: WebSockets vs polling vs server-sent events
What happens to your app when the connection drops
Conflict resolution when two people edit the same record

stages.title: C# and ASP.NET Core
stages.tagline: The same job, in the enterprise stack
stages.goal: Rebuild what you did in Node, in .NET — because half the CRUD jobs on the market are .NET jobs.
stages.outcome: You can hold a conversation about DI lifetimes, the middleware pipeline, and EF Core without bluffing.

modules.title: C# for people who know JavaScript
modules.why: The syntax is easy; the model is different. Value vs reference types and static typing change how you write, and both are early interview questions.
interviewFocus: Value types vs reference types, and where each lives
struct vs class vs record
What `null` means in C# 8+ nullable reference types

modules.title: LINQ, records, and pattern matching
modules.why: LINQ is C#'s superpower and its biggest performance footgun — deferred execution surprises people in interviews and in production.
interviewFocus: Deferred execution: when does the query actually run
IEnumerable vs IQueryable — and why it matters against a database
Records, `with` expressions, and value equality

modules.title: Interfaces, generics, and async
modules.why: Interfaces are how .NET does dependency injection, which is how .NET does everything. And `async` in C# has traps JavaScript doesn't.
interviewFocus: Interface vs abstract class — a real reason to pick each
Task vs Task<T> vs void async — and why `async void` is dangerous
ConfigureAwait, and whether you still need it

modules.title: ASP.NET Core: the pipeline and DI
modules.why: 'Explain the middleware pipeline' and 'what's the difference between scoped and transient' are the two most reliably asked .NET interview questions in existence.
interviewFocus: The middleware pipeline — order matters, and what happens if you get it wrong
Singleton vs scoped vs transient, and the captive-dependency bug
Model binding and where validation runs
ProblemDetails and a consistent error contract

modules.title: Data access and EF Core
modules.why: An ORM you don't understand will generate 400 queries and you won't know why. This module is mostly about making the ORM's behaviour visible.
interviewFocus: Change tracking — what it is and when to turn it off
Lazy vs eager vs explicit loading, and the N+1 it causes
Migrations: how schema change reaches production
Repository pattern over EF Core — worth it or not? Have an opinion

steps.title: Guide — ORMs, EF Core, and the queries they hide

modules.title: Config, auth, background work, and tests
modules.why: The parts of a .NET app that aren't endpoints. Configuration and hosted services come up whenever an interviewer wants to know if you've shipped.
interviewFocus: IOptions and where configuration comes from, in order
Where secrets live in development vs production
Background work: hosted services vs a real queue
Integration tests with WebApplicationFactory

modules.title: Fullstack .NET capstones
modules.why: Two complete applications, front to back. These are your portfolio pieces and the thing you'll actually talk about in an interview.
interviewFocus: Walk me through your project's architecture
What would you do differently if it had 100x the traffic
What was the hardest bug and how did you find it

stages.title: Shipping and being interviewed
stages.tagline: The half of the job that isn't writing code
stages.goal: Deploy something, observe it, debug it in production, and talk about all of it convincingly.
stages.outcome: You are mid-level: you can be handed a broken system you didn't write and make progress.

modules.title: Git, branches, and code review
modules.why: Everyone claims to know Git. Interviewers test it with 'you committed to the wrong branch, now what' and 'what does rebase do that merge doesn't'.
interviewFocus: merge vs rebase, and when rebasing is dangerous
How you'd undo: a bad commit, a bad push, a bad merge
What makes a pull request easy to review

steps.title: Guide — Git as it's actually used on a team

modules.title: Logging, metrics, and finding out what broke
modules.why: 'It works on my machine' is where a junior stops. Where a mid-level dev starts is: what do the logs say, what changed, and what's the blast radius.
interviewFocus: Structured logging and correlation ids
What you'd log at each level, and what must never be logged
How you'd debug a bug that only happens in production

steps.title: Guide — a debugging playbook for problems you didn't cause

modules.title: Performance and caching
modules.why: Caching questions ('where would you cache this, and how would you invalidate it') are a reliable mid-level filter because there is no memorisable right answer.
interviewFocus: The layers you could cache at, from browser to database
Cache invalidation strategies and their failure modes
How you'd find the bottleneck before optimising anything

steps.title: Guide — caching, from the browser to the database
Worker pool — using more than one core

modules.title: Environments, containers, and CI/CD
modules.why: You do not need to be a DevOps engineer. You do need to know what a Dockerfile is, why the pipeline is red, and how config differs between environments.
interviewFocus: What a container actually is (and isn't — it's not a VM)
How configuration and secrets differ between dev and prod
What a CI pipeline should run before a merge
Blue/green vs rolling deploys, and how you'd roll back

steps.title: Guide — Docker, enough to be useful
Guide — getting it onto the internet

modules.title: The interview itself
modules.why: Knowing the material and performing it are different skills. This module is about the second one.
interviewFocus: Walk me through a project you're proud of (2 minutes, structured)
Answering 'I don't know' well
Asking the questions that make you look senior
